exampleAnswers.title: Calculating Limits of Multivariable Functions at Points of Continuity

question.explanation:
Let the function $f(x,y)$ be defined as \[ f(x,y) = \sqrt[3]{3x - 2y + 1}. \]

The function $f(x,y)$ is continuous for all values of $x$ and $y.$ So, we can calculate the limit by substituting $(1,-2)$ into the function: \begin{align*} \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,-2)}} \sqrt[3]{3x - 2y + 1} & = \sqrt[3]{3(1) - 2(-2) + 1}\\[5pt] & = \sqrt[3]{3 + 4 + 1}\\[5pt] & = \sqrt[3]{8}\\[5pt] & = 2 \end{align*}

question.explanation:
Let the function $f(x,y)$ be defined as \[ f(x,y) = 2x - y + 3. \]

The function $f(x,y)$ is continuous for all values of $x$ and $y.$ So, we can calculate the limit by substituting $(-2,0)$ into the function: \begin{align*} \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (-2,0)}} (2x - y + 3) & = 2(-2) - 0 + 3\\[5pt] & = -4 - 0 + 3\\[5pt] & = -1 \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating Limits of Multivariable Functions at Points of Continuity

question.explanation:
Let the function $f(x,y)$ be defined as

\[ f(x,y)= \dfrac{x^2y^2}{x^3+y^3}. \]

The function $f(x,y)$ is continuous except when the denominator is zero. However, the point $(1,1)$ does not cause the denominator to vanish, so we can calculate the limit by substituting $(1,1)$ into the function:

\begin{align*} \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,1)}} \dfrac{x^2y^2}{x^3+y^3} = \dfrac{1^2\cdot1^2}{1^3+1^3} =\dfrac{1}{2} \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating Limits of Multivariable Rational Functions by Factoring

question.explanation:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\dfrac00,$ as follows:

\[ \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (2,2,-1)}} \dfrac{xyz-zy^2}{y^2-x^2} = \dfrac{2\cdot2\cdot(-1)-(-1)\cdot 2^2}{2^2-2^2} = \dfrac{0}{0} \]

However, we can simplify the limit by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

\begin{align} \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (2,2,-1)}} \dfrac{xyz-zy^2}{y^2-x^2} &= \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (2,2,-1)}} \dfrac{yz(x-y)}{-(x-y)(x+y)} \\[5pt] &= \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (2,2,-1)}} \dfrac{yz}{-x-y} \end{align}

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it using direct substitution:

\begin{align} \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (2,2,-1)}} \dfrac{yz}{-x-y} &= \dfrac{2\cdot(-1)}{-2-2}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{-2}{-4}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac12 \end{align}

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $\dfrac{1}{2}.$

example.title: Calculating Limits of Multivariable Rational Functions by Factoring

question.explanation:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\dfrac00,$ as follows:

\[ \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,2)}} \dfrac{x^2-xy}{x^3+2x} = \dfrac{0^2-0\cdot 2}{0^3-2 \cdot 0} = \dfrac{0}{0} \]

However, we can simplify the limit by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

\begin{align} \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,2)}} \dfrac{x^2-xy}{x^3+2x} &= \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,2)}} \dfrac{x(x-y)}{x(x^2+2)} \\[5pt] &= \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,2)}} \dfrac{x-y}{x^2+2} \end{align}

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it using direct substitution:

\begin{align} \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,2)}} \dfrac{x-y}{x^2+2} &= \dfrac{0-2}{0+2}\\[5pt] &=-1 \end{align}

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $-1.$

example.title: Calculating Limits of Multivariable Rational Functions by Factoring

question.explanation:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\dfrac00,$ as follows:

\[ \lim_{(x,y)\to (1,2)} \dfrac{2x^2+3xy-2y^2}{2x^2-xy} = \dfrac{2 \cdot 1^2 + 3 \cdot 1 \cdot 2 -2 \cdot 2^2}{2 \cdot 1^2 - 1 \cdot 2} = \dfrac{0}{0} \]

However, we can simplify the limit by first factoring the denominator, and then canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

\begin{align*} \lim_{(x,y)\to (1,2)} \dfrac{2x^2+3xy-2y^2}{2x^2-xy} &= \lim_{(x,y)\to (1,2)} \dfrac{2x^2 + 4xy - xy - 2y^2}{x(2x-y)} \\[5pt] &= \lim_{(x,y)\to (1,2)} \dfrac{2x(x + 2y) - y(x +2y)}{x(2x-y)} \\[5pt] &= \lim_{(x,y)\to (1,2)} \dfrac{(2x-y)(x+2y)}{x(2x-y)} \\[5pt] &= \lim_{(x,y)\to (1,2)} \dfrac{x+2y}{x} \end{align*}

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

\begin{align*} \displaystyle{\lim_{(x,y)\to (1,2)}} \dfrac{x+2y}{x} &= \dfrac{1+2 \cdot 2}{1} \\[5pt] &= 5 \end{align*}

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $5.$

example.title: Calculating Limits of Multivariable Rational Functions by Factoring

question.explanation:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0},$ as follows: \begin{align} \lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (-1,-1)} \dfrac{x^2 - y^2}{x^2 - xy} & = \dfrac{(-1)^2 - (-1)^2}{(-1)^2 - (-1)(-1)}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1 - 1}{1 - 1}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{0}{0} \end{align}

However, we can simplify the limit by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator: \begin{align} \require{cancel} \lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (-1,-1)} \dfrac{x^2 - y^2}{x^2 - xy} & = \lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (-1,-1)} \dfrac{(x + y)(x - y)}{x(x - y)} \\[5pt] & = \lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (-1,-1)} \dfrac{(x + y)\cancel{(x -y)}}{x\cancel{(x - y)}} \\[5pt] & = \lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (-1,-1)} \dfrac{x + y}{x} \end{align}

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it using direct substitution: \begin{align} \lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (-1,-1)} \dfrac{x + y}{x} & = \dfrac{-1 + (-1)}{(-1)}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{(-2)}{(-1)}\\[5pt] & = 2 \end{align}

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $2.$

example.title: Calculating Limits of Multivariable Rational Functions by Factoring

question.explanation:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\dfrac00,$ as follows:

\[ \displaystyle{\lim_{(x,y)\to (-1,1)}} \dfrac{2x^2+3xy+y^2}{x^3+xy+x^2y+y^2} = \dfrac{ 2 \cdot (-1)^2+3 \cdot (-1) \cdot 1 + 1^2}{(-1)^3 + (-1) \cdot 1 + (-1)^2 \cdot 1 + 1^2} = \dfrac{0}{0} \]

However, we can simplify the limit by factoring the numerator and denominator and then canceling common factors:

\begin{align*} \displaystyle{\lim_{(x,y)\to (-1,1)}} \dfrac{2x^2+3xy+y^2}{x^3+xy+x^2y+y^2} &= \displaystyle{\lim_{(x,y)\to (-1,1)}} \dfrac{2x^2+2xy+xy+y^2}{x^2(x+y)+y(x+y)}\\[5pt] &= \displaystyle{\lim_{(x,y)\to (-1,1)}} \dfrac{2x(x+y)+y(x+y)}{(x^2+y)(x+y)}\\[5pt] &= \displaystyle{\lim_{(x,y)\to (-1,1)}} \dfrac{(2x+y)(x+y)}{(x^2+y)(x+y)}\\[5pt] &= \displaystyle{\lim_{(x,y)\to (-1,1)}} \dfrac{2x+y}{x^2+y} \end{align*}

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

\begin{align*} \displaystyle{\lim_{(x,y)\to (-1,1)}} \dfrac{2x+y}{x^2+y} &= \dfrac{2(-1)+(1)}{(-1)^2+1} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac 12 \end{align*}

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $-\dfrac{1}{2}.$

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating Limits of Multivariable Functions Using Conjugate Multiplication

question.explanation:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0},$ as follows: \begin{align} \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (2,1,-1)} \dfrac{y + z}{\sqrt{x - y} - \sqrt{x + z}} & = \dfrac{1 + (-1)}{\sqrt{2 - 1} - \sqrt{2 + (-1)}}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1 - 1}{1 - 1}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{0}{0} \end{align}

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator: \begin{align*} \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x} \to (2,1,-1)} \dfrac{y + z}{\sqrt{x - y} - \sqrt{x + z}} & = \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (2,1,-1)} \dfrac{\left( y+z \right)\left( \sqrt{x - y} + \sqrt{x + z} \right)}{\left( \sqrt{x - y} - \sqrt{x + z} \right)\left( \sqrt{x - y} + \sqrt{x + z} \right)} \\[5pt] & = \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (2,1,-1)} \dfrac{\left( y+z \right)\left( \sqrt{x - y} + \sqrt{x + z} \right)}{ (x - y) - (x + z) } \\[5pt] & = \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (2,1,-1)} \dfrac{\left( y+z \right)\left( \sqrt{x - y} + \sqrt{x + z} \right)}{ -(y + z) } \\[5pt] & = -\lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (2,1,-1)} \dfrac{\cancel{\left( y+z \right)}\left( \sqrt{x - y} + \sqrt{x + z} \right)}{ \cancel{(y + z)} } \\[5pt] & = -\lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (2,1,-1)} \left( \sqrt{x - y} + \sqrt{x + z} \right) \end{align*}

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it: \begin{align*} -\lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (2,1,-1)} \left( \sqrt{x - y} + \sqrt{x + z} \right) & = -\left( \sqrt{2 - 1} + \sqrt{2 + (-1)} \right)\\[5pt] &= -(1 + 1)\\[5pt] & = -2 \end{align*}

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $-2.$

example.title: Calculating Limits of Multivariable Functions Using Conjugate Multiplication

question.explanation:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\dfrac00,$ as follows:

\[ \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (3,1, 2)}} \, \dfrac{ y-x+z}{\sqrt{x-z}-\sqrt {y}} = \dfrac{1-3+2} {\sqrt{3-2}-\sqrt {1}} = \dfrac{0}{0} \]

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

\begin{align*} \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (3,1, 2)}} \, \dfrac{ y-x+z}{\sqrt{x-z}-\sqrt y} &= \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to(3,1, 2)}} \, \dfrac{( y-x+z)\left(\sqrt{x-z}+\sqrt y\right)}{\left(\sqrt{x-z}-\sqrt y\right)\left(\sqrt{x-z}+\sqrt y\right)} \\[5pt] &= \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to(3,1, 2)}} \, \dfrac{( y-x+z)\left(\sqrt{x-z}+y\right)}{\left(\sqrt{x-z}\right)^2- \left(\sqrt y\right)^2} \\[5pt] &= \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to(3,1, 2)}} \, \dfrac{( y-x+z)\left(\sqrt{x-z}+y\right)}{x-z-y} \\[5pt] &= \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to(3,1, 2)}} \, \dfrac{-( x-z-y)\left(\sqrt{x-z}+y\right)}{x-z-y} \\[5pt] &= \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (3,1,2)}} -\left(\sqrt{x-z}+y\right) \end{align*}

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

\begin{align*} \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (3,1,2)}} -\left(\sqrt{x-z}+y\right) &= -\left(\sqrt{3-2}+1\right) \\[5pt] &=-(1+1) \\[5pt] &= -2 \end{align*}

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $-2.$

example.title: Calculating Limits of Multivariable Functions Using Conjugate Multiplication

question.explanation:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0},$ as follows: \begin{align} \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,0,1)} \dfrac{x + y - z^2}{\sqrt{x + y} - z} & = \dfrac{1 + 0 - 1^2}{\sqrt{1 + 0} - 1}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1 + 0 - 1}{1 - 1}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{0}{0} \end{align}

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator: \begin{align*} \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x} \to (1,0,1)} \dfrac{x + y - z^2}{\sqrt{x + y} - z} & = \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,0,1)} \dfrac{\big( x + y - z^2 \big)\big( \sqrt{x + y} + z\big)}{\big( \sqrt{x + y} - z\big)\big( \sqrt{x + y} + z\big)}\\[5pt] & = \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,0,1)} \dfrac{\big( x + y - z^2 \big)\big( \sqrt{x + y} + z\big)}{x + y - z^2}\\[5pt] & = \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,0,1)} \dfrac{\cancel{\big( x + y - z^2 \big)}\big( \sqrt{x + y} + z\big)}{\cancel{x + y - z^2}}\\[5pt] & = \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,0,1)} \big( \sqrt{x + y} + z \big) \end{align*}

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it: \begin{align*} \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,0,1)} \big(\sqrt{x + y} + z \big) & = \sqrt{1 + 0} + 1\\[5pt] & = 1 + 0 + 1\\[5pt] & = 2 \end{align*}

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $2.$

example.title: Calculating Limits of Multivariable Functions Using Conjugate Multiplication

question.explanation:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0},$ as follows: \begin{align} \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,2,-1)} \dfrac{x\sqrt{y+z} - 1}{x^2(y + z) - 1} & = \dfrac{1\sqrt{2 + (-1)} - 1}{(1^2)(2 + (-1)) - 1}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1 - 1}{1 - 1}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{0}{0} \end{align}

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the numerator: \begin{align*} \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x} \to (1,2,-1)} \dfrac{x\sqrt{y+z} - 1}{x^2(y + z) - 1} & = \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,2,-1)} \dfrac{\big(x\sqrt{y+z} - 1\big)\big(x\sqrt{y+z} + 1\big)}{\big(x^2(y + z) - 1\big)\big(x\sqrt{y+z} + 1\big)} \\[5pt] & = \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,2,-1)} \dfrac{x^2(y + z) - 1}{\big(x^2(y + z) - 1\big)\big(x\sqrt{y+z} + 1\big)}\\[5pt] & = \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,2,-1)} \dfrac{\cancel{x^2(y + z) - 1}}{\cancel{\big(x^2(y + z) - 1\big)}\big(x\sqrt{y+z} + 1\big)}\\[5pt] & = \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,2,-1)} \dfrac{1}{x\sqrt{y+z} + 1} \end{align*}

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it: \begin{align*} \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (1,2,-1)} \dfrac{1}{x\sqrt{y+z} + 1} & = \dfrac{1}{1\sqrt{2 + (-1)} + 1}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{1 + 1}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2} \end{align*}

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $\dfrac{1}{2}.$

example.title: Calculating Limits of Multivariable Functions Using Conjugate Multiplication

question.explanation:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0},$ as follows: \begin{align} \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (9,1,3)} \dfrac{x - y^2 z^2}{\sqrt{x} - yz} & = \dfrac{9 - (1^2)(3^2)}{\sqrt{9} - 1(3)}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{9 - 9}{3 - 3}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{0}{0} \end{align}

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator: \begin{align*} \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x} \to (9,1,3)} \dfrac{x - y^2 z^2}{\sqrt{x} - yz} & = \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (9,1,3)} \dfrac{\big( x - y^2 z^2 \big)\big( \sqrt{x} + yz\big)}{\big( \sqrt{x} - yz\big)\big( \sqrt{x} + yz\big)}\\[5pt] & = \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (9,1,3)} \dfrac{\big( x - y^2 z^2 \big)\big( \sqrt{x} + yz\big)}{x - y^2 z^2}\\[5pt] & = \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (9,1,3)} \dfrac{\cancel{\big( x - y^2 z^2 \big)}\big( \sqrt{x} + yz\big)}{\cancel{x - y^2 z^2}}\\[5pt] & = \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (9,1,3)} \big( \sqrt{x} + yz\big) \end{align*}

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it: \begin{align*} \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (9,1,3)} \big( \sqrt{x} + yz\big) & = \sqrt{9} + 1(3)\\[5pt] & = 3 + 3\\[5pt] & = 6 \end{align*}

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $6.$

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating Limits Along Different Paths for Multivariable Functions

question.explanation:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\dfrac00\mathbin{:}$

\[ \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)}} \, \dfrac{2y^2}{2x^2-y^2} = \dfrac{2\cdot 0^2}{2\cdot0^2- 0^2} = \dfrac{0}{0} \]

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

Let's attempt to evaluate the limit approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

  • Taking $\mathbf{x} \to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have \begin{align*} \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x} \to (0,0) \\ \:\: y=x}} \, \dfrac{2y^2}{2x^2-y^2} &= \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0}}\, \dfrac{2x^2}{2x^2-x^2}\\ &= \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0}} \, \dfrac{2x^2}{x^2}\\[5pt] &= \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0}} \, 2 \\[5pt] &= 2. \end{align*}

  • Taking $\mathbf{x} \to (0,0)$ along the line $y= 0$ (the $x$-axis), we have
    \begin{align*} \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x} \to (0,0) \\ \:\: y= 0}} \, \dfrac{2y^2}{2x^2-y^2} &=\displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x} \to 0}} \, \dfrac{2\cdot 0^2}{2x^2-0^2}\\ &= \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0}}\, 0\\[5pt] &= 0. \end{align*}

Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

\[ \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)}} \, \dfrac{2y^2}{2x^2-y^2}= \textrm{DNE} \]

example.title: Calculating Limits Along Different Paths for Multivariable Functions

question.explanation:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\dfrac00\mathbin{:}$

\[ \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)}} \, \dfrac{xy}{2x^2+3y^2} = \dfrac{0\cdot 0}{2\cdot 0^2+ 3\cdot 0^2} = \dfrac{0}{0} \]

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

Let's attempt to evaluate the limit approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

  • Taking $\mathbf{x} \to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have \begin{align*} \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x} \to (0,0) \\ \:\: y=x}} \, \dfrac{xy}{2x^2+3y^2} &= \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0}}\, \dfrac{x^2}{2x^2+3x^2}\\ &= \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0}} \, \dfrac{x^2}{5x^2}\\[5pt] &= \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0}} \, \dfrac15 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac15. \end{align*}

  • Taking $\mathbf{x} \to (0,0)$ along the line $y= -x$, we have
    \begin{align*} \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x} \to (0,0) \\ \:\: y= -x}} \,\dfrac{xy}{2x^2+3y^2} &= \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0}}\, \dfrac{-x^2}{2x^2+3x^2}\\ &= \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0}} \, \dfrac{-x^2}{5x^2}\\[5pt] &= \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0}} \, \left (-\dfrac15\right ) \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac15. \end{align*}

Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

\[ \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)}} \, \dfrac{xy}{2x^2+3y^2} = \textrm{DNE} \]

example.title: Calculating Limits Along Different Paths for Multivariable Functions

question.text:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the limit given below? \[ \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)}} \dfrac{y}{x^2+2y} \]

  1. The limit evaluates to $\dfrac 13$ along the path $y=x^2$
  2. The limit evaluates to $-1$ along the path $y=-x^2$
  3. The limit exists and is equal to $\dfrac 13$
question.explanation:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\dfrac00\mathbin{:}$

\[ \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)}} \dfrac{y}{x^2+2y} = \dfrac{0}{0^2+2\cdot0}= \dfrac{0}{0} \]

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

  • Statement I is true. Taking $\mathbf{x} \to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x^2,$ we have \begin{align*} \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x} \to (0,0) \\ \:\: y=x^2}} \dfrac{y}{x^2+2y} &= \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0}} \dfrac{x^2}{x^2+2x^2}\\[5pt] &= \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0}} \dfrac{x^2}{3x^2}\\[5pt] &= \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0}} \dfrac{1}{3}\\[3pt] &= \dfrac 13 \end{align*}

  • Statement II is false. Taking $\mathbf{x} \to (0,0)$ along the path $y=-x^2,$ we have \begin{align*} \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x} \to (0,0) \\ \:\: y=-x^2}} \dfrac{y}{x^2+2y} &= \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0}} \dfrac{-x^2}{x^2+2(-x^2)}\\[3pt] &= \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0}} \dfrac{-x^2}{-x^2}\\[3pt] &= 1. \end{align*}

  • Statement III is false. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist: \[ \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)}} \dfrac{y}{x^2+2y} = \text{DNE} \]

question.explanation:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0}\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align} \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)} \dfrac{x^2 - y^2}{x^2 + y^2} & = \dfrac{0^2 - 0^2}{0^2 + 0^2}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{0 - 0}{0 + 0}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{0}{0} \end{align}

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

Let's attempt to evaluate the limit approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

  • Taking $\mathbf{x} \to (0,0)$ along the path $y = 0,$ we have \begin{align*} \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x} \to (0,0) \\ \:\: y = 0} \dfrac{x^2 - y^2}{x^2 + y^2} & = \lim\limits_{x \to 0} \dfrac{x^2 - 0^2}{x^2 + 0^2}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{x^2}{x^2}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to 0} 1\\[5pt] & = 1. \end{align*}

  • Taking $\mathbf{x} \to (0,0)$ along the path $y = x,$ we have \begin{align*} \lim\limits_{\mathbf{x} \to (0,0) \\ \:\: y=x} \dfrac{x^2 - y^2}{x^2 + y^2} & = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{x^2 - x^2}{x^2 + x^2}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{0}{2x^2}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{x \to 0} 0\\[5pt] & = 0 \end{align*}

Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist: \[ \lim_{\mathbf{x} \to (0,0)} \dfrac{x^2 - y^2}{x^2 + y^2} = \textrm{DNE} \]

question.explanation:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\dfrac00\mathbin{:}$

\[ \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)}} \, \dfrac{2yx^3}{x^6+8y^2} = \dfrac{2\cdot 0\cdot 0^3}{0^6+8\cdot 0^2} = \dfrac{0}{0} \]

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

Let's attempt to evaluate the limit approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

  • Taking $\mathbf{x} \to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have \begin{align*} \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x} \to (0,0) \\ \:\: y=x}} \, \dfrac{2yx^3}{x^6+8y^2} &= \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0}}\, \dfrac{2x^4}{x^6+8x^2}\\ &= \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0}} \, \dfrac{2x^4}{x^2 (x^4+ 8)}\\[5pt] &= \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0}} \, \dfrac{2x^2}{x^4+ 8} \\[5pt] &= 0. \end{align*}

  • Taking $\mathbf{x} \to (0,0)$ along the path $y= x^3,$ we have
    \begin{align*} \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x} \to (0,0) \\ \:\: y= x^3}} \, \dfrac{2yx^3}{x^6+8y^2} &= \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0}}\, \dfrac{2x^6}{x^6+8x^6}\\[5pt] &= \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0}} \, \dfrac{2x^6}{9x^6}\\[5pt] &= \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to 0}} \, \dfrac{2}{9} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 29. \end{align*}

Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

\[ \displaystyle{\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to (0,0)}} \, \dfrac{2yx^3}{x^6+8y^2}= \textrm{DNE} \]
